In a press release coinciding with Grand Theft Auto VI becoming available for pre-load ahead of its November 19th release date, Rockstar has confirmed that the game "has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits." Read between the lines, and you can kind of make out the words "...so hope your PCs are up to spec, computer nerds.".

Industry observers note that GTA 6, of course, still does not have a confirmed PC version, even if Rockstar's former tech director says it's probably not far off. And despite this, even ancient, last-gen consoles are getting in on it, as the release also unexpectedly confirms that the game will be playable on Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming, Microsoft's game streaming service that has suddenly lost its ability to work on PC. Granted, this comes with a warning: "as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay." If you ended up getting a PS4 last generation, no cloud play for you either, I'm afraid. It also states that it will "play best on Playstation 5 consoles", making great use of that Sony partnership, and will include Playstation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows on PS5 Pro.

It has been revealed that A 2026 current-gen game targeting 30fps, let alone one as titanic of a release as GTA VI, is probably not going to go down well with a lot of people, even if console players are traditionally les sensitive about FPS counts than PC players. What this does imply, though, is that the inevitable PC release might be an even more demanding behemoth than expected, if Xbox Series and PS5 versions can't even target 60fps. The availability of the game on Xbox One, even if just through cloud streaming, could have resulted in an acceptance that 60fps just wasn't going to be possible if it was also going to be able to 'run' on last-gen hardware. Either way, when it does eventually escape console exclusivity, hopefully trying to run GTA VI on anything less than an RTX 5080 won't set your PC on fire. Now, let me just quickly have a glance at GPU prices. Oh, no.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Significant Walk.
  • In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Significant Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Substantial Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer said. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.".

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, challenges we encountered with third-party code.".

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

House House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.".

House House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Recent findings suggest that "Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.".

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Major Walk review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's finally here! We've officially reached the launch week of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, PS5 and even the Xbox One (kind of), 13 long years since the most recent entry in the series back in 2013.

With that in mind, we thought we'd put up a quick release times guide so you know exactly when you can start playing the game, and we've also thrown in a few extra details about what we're expecting for Xbox One players at launch.

So, here are all the deets you need to know for Thursday!

The official GTA 6 release date is Thursday, November 19th. You may still see people playing it on Wednesday though, as depending on where you live, certain players will be getting access to it earlier than others.

In a recent development, GTA 6 releases at midnight local time around the world. This means you'll be able to start playing it on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S and PS5 as soon as November 18th turns into November 19th in your region.

In a recent development, the only exception to the rule may be in countries with multiple time zones. For example, Rockstar seems to be classing "midnight" based around the EST time zone in the US, which would mean PST gets it at 9pm on the 18th.

Technically, yes. Due to the staggered rollout, players in New Zealand will be getting first access to GTA 6 at midnight in their time zone, which equates to 11am on November 18th here in the UK, and even earlier in the United States.

We urge caution around this, as Xbox's terms of service specifically state that you shouldn't switch regions unless you're actually located in the country you're switching to, but we'll leave the decision up to you.

You may have noticed that we didn't mention Xbox One in the release times section up above, and that's because we don't quite know what's happening with it. In a nutshell, Xbox One players will be forced to use Xbox Cloud Gaming in order to get access to GTA 6, which in theory should require buying the game before access is granted.

There are too many unknowns ahead of launch about how this works though. Will cloud access be made available immediately? Will you be able to use the free-with-ads version of the cloud to play GTA 6, or will it require paying for the service? Is it just Xbox One that you can play it on, or will mobile and PC devices be supported too?

That's where we stand ahead of launch, so while GTA 6 definitely will be playable through the cloud on Xbox One in some form, it's probably best to wait until it's been released before handing over any money as things stand.

Of course, we've already talked about the preload for GTA 6 and how anyone can download the game right now on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, regardless of whether they've actually bought it or not.

All that's left is to wait a few more days until the new Grand Theft Auto finally becomes available, and we can't wait to see whether it'll live up to the hype and become a Game of the Year contender when it arrives this Thursday.

Any other questions about the release plans for GTA 6 on Xbox? Leave them in the comments below.

But for a small selection of true enthusiasts, the game is already working on mobile and handheld devices.

One such person showing off WoW: Forever on the go is none other than director of publishing at Larian, Michael Douse, who took to Twitter to show off the MMO being played on an AYN Thor device. For those who don't know, this is a fancy android handheld console, a sort of beefed up DS for the modern handheld aficionado.

In a recent development, "Arguably too many layers of abstraction," writes Douse. In the picture he posted, you can see the player character viewable on the Thor's top screen, while the map, text chat, skill UI, and buffs viewable on the bottom. It looks pretty cool, and is made possible due to JReese702's Github mod you can download at your leisure.

Arguably too many layers of abstraction pic.twitter.com/VjW0IX00Gg.

But it's not the only mo-bell at the ball. Another Github WoW: Forever mod, WolkaraForever, gets the game playable on the iPhone Duo. As highlighted by CEO of esports company 100 Thieves Alex Wechsler on Twitter, the game looks to be ported pretty well to the phone, with mobile touchscreen controls viewable on both sides of the screen. Be warned though, as confirmed by Wechsler in a Twitter reply, it'll get your phone running hot.

As a father of 2 kids and always having wanted to play WOW, I’ve finally found a way 🥹 pic.twitter.com/eIVn0gn1WC.

It has been revealed that this coming alongside World of Warcraft: Forever's built-in (and very good) controller support could mean the game has real potential to spread far and wide across the vast array of different hardware out there. Blizzard has already hinted at plans of porting the game to other platforms, so who knows? Maybe we can expect an official mobile port to tread the path paved by these community-made mods.

#28428. Industry News: Talking Point: As A Parent, What Worries You Most About Gaming?

Industry News: Talking Point: As A Parent, What Worries You Most About Gaming?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nintendolife

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids.
  • I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.
  • Recent findings suggest that I worried their attention might wander while watching for 30-60 minutes at a time, and I don't want to be that parent, forcing something I loved on my disinterested kids ("What do you mean 'Thunderbirds is boring'?!").
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids. I hadn't intended to, but it dawned on me that once the gorgeous remake landed, the original's visible polygons might not hold the same appeal for them. It was selfish, really, but I wanted them to experience the original magic as I did.

I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.

Recent findings suggest that I worried their attention might wander while watching for 30-60 minutes at a time, and I don't want to be that parent, forcing something I loved on my disinterested kids ("What do you mean 'Thunderbirds is boring'?!"). I was ready to pull the cord if they didn't take to it.

But no! They were pointing and problem-solving alongside me, jumping up and down, utterly engaged and loving the story and our shared experience.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the screen, Ocarina provoked laughter over dinner, and discussion about why characters reacted as they did, the cause and effect of actions, and the resulting emotions. Car journeys suddenly had a newly introduced soundtrack accompaniment, and the game's themes would come up while drawing or playing with Lego or finding a 'Deku' stick out on a walk. It became a rich source of inspiration for their imaginations, and a springboard to conversation and closeness with my kids. A fantastic family adventure we'll remember for years to come.

It's such a shame, then, when you see parents whose kids love games struggle to recognise the benefits and sheer joy they can bring, and potentially miss out on family experiences like mine. For something so ubiquitous and so fun, gaming can create real tension in the home and throw up generational barriers that take time and understanding to break down.

And with all the online concerns and other ills of the modern age, it's easy to see why some parents might perceive games as a dead-end, dangerous time sink that needs to be contained and quarantined, like fast food or social media.

According to a recent Ofcom report, 88% of children aged 3-17 in the UK play games on some form of device, and given Nintendo's evergreen, all-ages remit to deliver surprise and delight, addressing concerns of gaming-cautious guardians is something the manufacturer is keen on, beyond the bare minimum of secure account systems and Parental Control tools.

So that'll be why they've partnered up with Andy Robertson, founder of the Family Gaming Database and longtime friend of the site, for the recently published Parent's Guide to Gaming with Confidence.

Longtime Nintendo Life readers may recognise Andy from the various articles and reviews he's penned for us over the years, or from our partnership with Family Gaming to highlight accessibility information in our reviews and game pages across the network.

Produced in association with Nintendo, in this newly introduced guide Andy has also enlisted other experts in the fields of gaming, child psychology, and online safety to help parents of all gaming backgrounds digest the key questions and perhaps reframe how some of them view video games.

Available as a downloadable PDF, Andy explores common misconceptions and offers sound advice from expert contributors, including child psychologist Dr Amanda Gummer and Dr Catherine Knibbs, a child and adult psychotherapist specialising in online harm.

As you'll see from the breakout boxes on this page, uncertainties about other online players and predatory monetisation systems are the main sources of anxiety for NL staff with kids. "I'm very concerned about exploitative mechanics," states Alex, our senior video producer, "things designed to get their hooks into people's brains and make them dependent, or cough up wads of cash.".

According to Ofcom's research, these are common worries:.

Industry observers note that the biggest type of concern among parents and carers of 3-17-year-olds who play games online is their child talking to strangers through games or via the chat functions (64%). This is followed by concerns about bullying by other players (60%), exposure to inappropriate content such as violence, bad language or disturbing material (59%), and pressure to make in-game purchases (51%).

Dr Knibbs highlights how "digital spaces can feel less familiar" than physical play spaces like playgrounds. The dangers can be less obvious, too, although she stresses that understanding the risks is better than avoidance. "When we learn about the content, the people and the spaces our children are engaging with, we are much better placed to help them navigate those experiences safely and positively.".

According to recent reports, it's not just about risk assessment, but also realising the potential benefits - and that doesn't require extensive gaming experience. "The goal ISN’T to become a gamer," Andy writes. "It is to better understand the people you care about most." You don't need to have conquered Elden Ring or any other game to participate and 'get' games.

Another key point to stress to non-gaming parents might seem almost self-evident, but it's easily overlooked if recognising Mario and Pac-Man represents your sum knowledge of the medium.

For some, even now, 'gaming' remains an arcade-style competition for high scores, and that can create a disconnect between parents with preconceived notions and their kids, who are discovering that games can be so much more.

"A child who is creating, collaborating, problem-solving or connecting with friends is having a very different experience from someone passively consuming content," Dr Amanda Gummer writes in a section of the guide highlighting "one of the most common mistakes parents make" - that all games are essentially the same.

We can all recall 'Wow, games can do this???' moments when the scales fell from our eye. It might have been an emotional beat in Shadow of the Colossus, or a surprising Wii Sports session with grandparents over the holidays; whatever the source, getting the uninitiated to that point is a crucial first step. While it's all notionally 'reading', hopping between Wikipedia articles is obviously not the same as reading a poem or sitting down with James Patterson's latest or doomscrolling social media feeds or taking a crack at Ulysses, and once parents understand that the world of video games is equally expansive, they've got a foundation to build upon.

It has been revealed that andy takes time to break down what he terms "the myth of the isolated gamer" and how, in fact, games can bring families together. Living the Nintendo life as we do, multiplayer has been commonplace for decades, but the lone gamer in the basement/attic stereotype persists.

Likewise — and this has long been a personal bugbear when talking with friends and family — rationing 'screen time' feels like an oversimplification for parents guarding against passive media consumption. Lamenting how young people these days don't get enough fresh air is absolutely valid, and getting out in the park, playground, and beyond is crucial to a child's overall development, but it's not as simple as 'outside=good, inside=bad'. The storytelling, learning, collaboration, creativity, and deep experiences games can offer are enormously valuable.

As Andy points out, "understanding the quality of the experience is often more useful than simply counting the minutes." Bowling in Switch Sports, having the national news on in the background, diving into a Mario world, and throwing Bluey on Disney+ are all different types of 'screen time', each with their own benefits and potential drawbacks.

You may not have noticed, but Nintendo Life has grown recently. Behind the scenes, we've had new additions to the family, with two team members recently joining the ranks of Hookshot Media parentdom.

Across our editorial, video, and management teams, our collective tribe runs the age gamut from newborn to undergrad, so we've got a broad range of experience, making it fairly simple to gauge what's appropriate for our kids, suggest games they might like (or slyly leave them lying around to be 'discovered') while monitoring interactions and steering them towards the all-timers (hi, Ocarina) and, importantly, away from less healthy, obsessive patterns that we may have fallen into in our youth.

And yes, there are certain games, primarily targeting younger gamers, that we wouldn't install on any device in the house.

It has been revealed that authorities in some territories are taking steps to mitigate the potential harm of the aggressive monetisation systems baked into platforms like Roblox. In the last week, the EU published its Digital Fairness Act proposal, which could impact any game featuring in-game purchases in the EU. Among other things, the bloc is seeking to curtail "addictive design", "dark patterns", and predatory monetisation tactics.

The DFA would only affect players in Europe, but regulation that forces real currency prices and lootbox odds to be displayed, those and similar systems defaulting to 'off' for minors, and parental consent being required to activate them are all positive steps.

While legislation could mean substantial changes for some developers and publishers, it's unlikely to cause Nintendo itself headaches.

With first-party software, in-game purchases are typically limited to DLC expansions or Switch 2 Upgrade Packs, and content-wise, it's a rare Nintendo game that I wouldn't feel comfortable playing with my kids in the room - something our teams over on Push Square and Pure Xbox have to be more cautious about, I'd wager.

Sources indicate that every kid is different, of course. Some may not be phased at all by a lurching ReDead in Hyrule Castle Town, while others might be kept up at night after glimpsing a creepy icon on the home screen. Handily, Switch's handheld hybrid format does make it easier to take the game away from the living room if, say, you need half an hour with Resident Evil Requiem away from eager eyes, and the console's aforementioned Parental Controls and accompanying app make monitoring the kids' gaming pretty simple.

In a recent development, communicating to nervous parents not just the risks but the rewards is something we're passionate about on the team, and that's something that Andy's guide does particularly well. "Failure is a part of success," he writes. "Games create safe environments where mistakes are expected. This can help children build resilience without even realising it. Every setback becomes part of learning." Makes me feel better about all the times the dogs got me in Call of Duty.

Confidence is a key term. Naturally, it's in Nintendo's interest to maintain its carefully curated family-friendly image, but giving parents who aren't embedded in the ins and outs of the gaming scene the confidence to engage is a win for the medium and everyone who loves it. A digestible guide like this for game-sceptic family and friends could come in handy over the holidays.

(To be clear, I'm not advocating becoming a gaming missionary at the dinner table and forcing pamphlets on relatives. But, you know, slyly leaving them lying around to be 'discovered' and having Switch Sports Resort ready to go after dessert? A round of golf and some bowling has worked wonders in the past!).

As with anything, a good grasp of the complications is essential, and every parent and child will have their own approaches, preferences, and ideas. For the NL team, though — and for me personally — sharing how games can enrich our family lives regardless of experience and ability is important. By alleviating concerns and highlighting benefits, we can open doors for latest players and experience more of those treasured 'Oh, games can do this???' moments together.

What worries you most as a parent? Which games have you played and enjoyed the most with your kids? Let us know your thoughts in the polls below, and feel free to take to the comments to share your experiences and the effect gaming has in your family.

Bandai Namco is liquidating Unknown 9: Awakening studio Reflector Entertainment, following multiple previous layoffs since the game's launch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco revealed in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening.
  • According to recent reports, the press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year.
  • It has been revealed that bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now.

As another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco revealed in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening. In its notice, Bandai Namco explains that the reason for the liquidation is due to Reflector not meeting its expectations for "future business looks, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation.".

According to recent reports, the press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year. This is not the first time Reflector has been cut by Bandai, as around a month after the launch of Unknown 9: Awakening and presumably in response to its low sales, 18% of the workforce was laid off. 2025 then saw further redundancies amidst the cancellation of a prospective project, though details on those layoffs were not granted by the company. Unknown 9 was intended to be a transmedia franchise involving the game as well as comic books and novels, but these ambitions never came to pass.

It has been revealed that bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now. A similar process faces Arkane Lyon, which is currently in a purgatory of having been chosen for closure by Microsoft, but temporarily protected by French labor laws that prevent it from being suddenly closed without proper negotiation and procedure.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a significant expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her significant gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Sources indicate that beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

It has been revealed that this revision will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A few things come to mind when I think about what the greatest fear of a Battlefield player is. It could be a glint atop the mountains on Liberation Peak, reliving the launch of Battlefield 2042, or maybe it's the randomised recoil from the first Battlefield. All of these are good bets, but I think the real shared nightmare of most Battlefield players is that someday it'll morph into Call of Duty.

In a recent development, to be fair, this fear isn't entirely unfounded. Bryan Beede was previously appointed as Battlefield's general manager after spending 19 years working on Call of Duty and has now been promoted to group general manager at EA. Taking his place is another Call of Duty veteran, Sam Cooper, who worked as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

Recent findings suggest that "I'm excited to share that I've joined Electronic Arts as general manager of Battlefield," Cooper states in a LinkedIn post. "I started my games career at EA on the FIFA team, so coming back to where it all began feels extra special.

"Battlefield is an iconic franchise that has something no other shooter has: all-out warfare, destruction at massive scale, squads play, and a passionate community that has stuck with this franchise for more than two decades.".

Now this in and of itself isn't enough to sound any alarm bells for players concerned whether or not Battlefield can stay true to form, especially since Beede was appointed as Battlefield GM back in 2021 prior to Battlefield 6's release. But this alongside some questionable new skins has some Battlefield players worried that Battlefield is becoming more "en-cod-ified".

A massive talking point during Battlefield 6's launch was players begging the devs to ignore COD's trend of gimmicky skins and instead stay true to its in-game realism for cosmetics. This has largely been the case—although the Dead Space collab was a near miss. But now some believe the cracks are starting to show with the latest Fox Hunter skin pack.

"There's absolutely no way you can defend this," one player claims in response to the skin pack. "There's a pseudo furry skin in Battlefield now. The defense I've heard is that 'it's plausible', while these are plausible, the masks are just, no? What tactical purpose does wearing a Japanese baby mask [or] a furry mask serve?" I'd argue, however, that it could stun an enemy Battlefield player long enough for you to secure a kill, and therefore there's at least some tactical purpose to it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Raiders, Embark Studios' popular extraction shooter, has exceeded 17m copies sold, according to publisher Nexon.

Arc Raiders was released at the end of October 2025, so reaching that milestone in a year is nothing to scoff at. According to Nexon's latest earnings report, however, only 1m copies of those 17 were sold in the third quarter - meaning sales have certainly slowed down.

It has been revealed that relatedly, Nexon said it expects Arc Raiders' revenue to decline in the fourth quarter compared to the same period last year - when the game enjoyed its hugely successful launch - and anticipates revenue will be "broadly flat sequentially". Despite this, the company said Arc Raiders' revenue was "within the outlook", naming its Frozen Trail upgrade as a key moment that brought back some lapsed players while introducing latest ones.

Indeed, Frozen Trail boosted the game's Steam player count, and reports suggest it also helped Arc Raiders hit a six-month player high across various platforms.

Recent findings suggest that even with its slowing sales, Arc Raiders remains one of Nexon's most successful titles. The firm primarily attributed an overall year-on-year revenue increase, for the nine months ended 30th September, to the game.

In a recent development, looking ahead, the biggest question hanging over Arc Raiders is whether or not it's going to get a dedicated PvE playlist. Following a successful test earlier this summer, Embark has been coy, and hasn't said whether PvE will return as a permanent feature. Arc Raiders' Chinese version does have a dedicated PvE mode, and executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said he could see both PvP and PvE modes co-existing in the future.

Organization of Heroes 3 developer admits "it was a lot" to make the 3.0 overhaul patch alongside regular updates, singleplayer DLC, and a whole spinoff game

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Manufacturer of Heroes 3's 3.0 upgrade is huge.
  • Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 revision's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.
  • It has been revealed that the team began planning the 3.0 enhancement two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Firm of Heroes 3, and focus on issues players had flagged since launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Manufacturer of Heroes 3's 3.0 upgrade is huge. Touching virtually every part of the three-year-old RTS, the patch notes are longer than, well, my arm isn't a great measure of patch note length. Let's just say the headline features of overhauled VFX and audio don't really cover it. It also comes with latest autumn and winter biomes, an updated grand strategy campaign, improvements to unit AI, and a whole host of other changes.

Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 revision's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.

It has been revealed that the team began planning the 3.0 enhancement two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Firm of Heroes 3, and focus on issues players had flagged since launch. "The VFX were called out," executive producer Denise Christie tells me. "Same thing with a lot of our audio.".

Relic were already releasing patches every three months, but the changes they were looking at were much too large for those smaller updates. If they had tried to do the work as part of the small updates, approaching the problems with piecemeal solutions, it would have turned Firm of Heroes 3 into a hodgepodge of new and old assets. "We wanted to make sure it was a cohesive package," principal designer Eric Wrobel says. "If you increase the quality of one thing, you have to do it equally across so much stuff." Otherwise you end up with "One that looks awesome and one that's like, 'Oh, this one's kind of gross'.".

Complicating matters, though, was that the team couldn't down tools and focus on just these large changes. As well as the small patches that were still going out every three months, both the VFX and audio teams were also contributing the battlegroup DLC packs which added upcoming units to the game. "They would work on stuff and in one branch that was the 3.0 work and then they would go ahead and do some battlegroup stuff and come back to that," Christie claims. "It was a lot.".

According to recent reports, as the 3.0 revision grew in scope, it also meant other departments were contributing to the anniversary release while working on the smaller updates and DLC. "For us to create future maps for Organization of Heroes 3, we were going to have an issue that our assets were getting stale," Christie explains. So, as part of 3.0, Relic's art department created autumn and winter asset packs, as well as a fresh Industrial theme. This then created more work for the VFX team, who have added rain and snow, as well as a transition effect showing soil and concrete moving from dry to wet.

Industry observers note that not to be outdone, the design team also made significant changes to the singleplayer Italy campaign. The towns that dot the dynamic grand strategy-inspired map now have individual upgrades, making for more meaningful decisions when it comes to which settlement you capture next. And, responding to one of the main criticisms of Company of Heroes 3's singleplayer, they also updated the computer's AI so it makes smarter decisions in both the turn-based and real-time battles. "We wanted to get this feel like there was that sort of back and forth of the AI resisting you and pushing forward into your territory and actually taking your stuff, which wasn't really happening in any of the previous updates," Wrobel claims.

Further complicating matters was the fact that alongside these regular updates, the DLC, and the substantial 3.0 revision release work, was that Relic also released Final Stand in July, a roguelike horde mode spinoff of Firm of Heroes 3. "We had to be very careful not to accidentally introduce this 3.0 work that was also happening at the same time," Christie claims." The improvements in this update have also rolled out for the spinoff, too.

It has been revealed that naturally, Relic aren't doing all this work purely out of the goodness of the hearts. The regular updates keep players engaged, Christie explains, and "hopefully bring back lapsed players who were frustrated by some of these things." It's something the team have already seen happen before, Wrobel explains. "We saw with the 2.0 update that we had a substantial spike of people and that was great, but because that improved the overall quality of the game, we saw each month we were selling more copies than we were before. People have been buying these games for years and years and years, so if we invest in this now we're going to see returns for quite a long time into the future as well.".

"If we were starting to see that tail down then we probably would have made a very different decision to be honest, but that's not what we see," Christie adds.

The next release for Firm of Heroes 3 is a singleplayer DLC, Operation Torch, due out on November 25th. (So, if you're keeping count, that was also in the works while the update, battlegroup DLC, and spinoff were all being made.) Until now, Relic's additions to the RTS have been focused on the multiplayer community, adding latest units to be used online or in offline skirmishes. Operation Torch brings new scripted missions that trace a set of soldiers moving through North Africa.

After that, though, I ask if Relic plans to continue adding to Company of Heroes 3 or if they're ready to move onto a fresh project. "Well, it's both actually," CEO Justin Dowdeswell tells me. "We would love to continue with Company of Heroes 3 and not solely as a place for us to experiment. That's one of the advantages of being smaller, and being able to make decisions. We're not going to leave Company of Heroes 3. It's an and function. We are going to embark on the next thing.".

So, it doesn't sound like Relic are taking anything off their plate….

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Valve has released a latest Steam upgrade that adds Steam Deck framerate data to a game's store page, giving potential buyers an indication of how well a game runs on the handheld.
  • It has been revealed that as per Valve's announcement post, average framerates are now listed in the Steam Deck Compatibility section of a game's store page, but you'll need to click Learn More to see it.
  • According to recent reports, according to Valve, average framerates are derived from players running the game on their Steam Decks, assuming they've opted in to provide framerate data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Valve has released a latest Steam upgrade that adds Steam Deck framerate data to a game's store page, giving potential buyers an indication of how well a game runs on the handheld.

It has been revealed that as per Valve's announcement post, average framerates are now listed in the Steam Deck Compatibility section of a game's store page, but you'll need to click Learn More to see it. Additionally, the feature is only available for games that have been tested for Deck compatibility - those with Verified, Playable, or Unsupported badges - so while it's not a complete list, it still covers thousands of titles.

According to recent reports, according to Valve, average framerates are derived from players running the game on their Steam Decks, assuming they've opted in to provide framerate data. And the store widget also includes another helpful addition: a histogram displaying the percentage of data samples. This shows how often a particular framerate has been reported, and is useful in determining if the game's framerate is sporadic, such as due to stutters.

"The current Steam Deck Verified compatibility rating is based on standardised test criteria, but it may not match every customer's bar for acceptable gameplay," Valve explained of the new feature.

"This is especially true around performance - a game with an Unsupported rating due to unstable performance may be considered playable by some customers, and a Verified game may not reach a framerate that some customers prefer to play at. By providing average framerate data for each game, customers now have a more complete picture of how the game performs on Steam Deck and can make more informed purchase and play decisions.".

Industry observers note that currently, Steam's framerate data feature only covers performance on Steam Deck, and for a very good reason: Valve's handheld has standardised hardware, so the results will be the same for all players. However, Valve states it intends to provide framerate data for more devices in the future, but it's not clear if that's ever going to include desktop PCs, considering the complex nature of their hardware configurations.

Recent findings suggest that if I wasn't so sick of hearing about AI every day of my life at the moment I might have found it funny to hear that one of the biggest peddlers of the poison around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Oh who am I kidding, it is funny! And despite knowing that this won't likely push Nvidia away from AI, I am a bit tickled to hear that the tech company and Huang are on the receiving end of a lawsuit.

Industry observers note that the suit in question, as reported by The Guardian, is based on a complaint filed in California's federal court on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher by Rosen Law Firm. Kistenmacher is an Nvidia shareholder, and with this suit he's seeking to "recover compensable damages," for himself and other shareholders due to the "precipitous decline in the market value of the Tech giant’s securities." What a palaver! I do not imagine this will be resolved particularly quickly.

As it at the moment stands, Huang has only admitted to having an affair rather than any trade secrets being leaked anywhere. Nvidia had this to say on the matter: "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.".

In a recent development, the concern comes from the person Huang had an affair with, one Alice Huang (no, they aren't related), a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm who have allegedly given Chinese companies Nvidia chips they bought billions of US dollars of. A messy situation to be sure, and one I unconfidently hope brings about the end of AI, somehow.

#28417. "30fps makes sense" for GTA 6, tech analyst claims, and anything above that is "asking for trouble"

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (711 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gamesradar ↗ Open Full Page

"30fps makes sense" for GTA 6, tech analyst claims, and anything above that is "asking for trouble"

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that rockstar presented GTA 6 at 30fps in every trailer going back years, so it's little surprise that the game will run at that frame rate.
  • Industry observers note that "You've got to consider the frame time budgets," according to Richard Leadbetter of Digital Foundry in a recent podcast discussion.
  • Sources indicate that "At 30fps they've got 33.3 milliseconds to process the game world, the simulation, all of that stuff," Leadbetter explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rockstar presented GTA 6 at 30fps in every trailer going back years, so it's little surprise that the game will run at that frame rate. But there was some hope that an upgraded console like the PS5 Pro could push things up to at least 40fps, yet Rockstar has apparently confirmed that the PS5 Pro has the same 30fps cap as every other platform. Tech analysts suggest that any frame rate above 30 is likely not feasible for a game as ambitious as Rockstar's latest.

Industry observers note that "You've got to consider the frame time budgets," according to Richard Leadbetter of Digital Foundry in a recent podcast discussion. While we, as players, tend to think of frame rates purely in terms of frames per second, game developers have to consider how long it takes to create each individual frame.

Sources indicate that "At 30fps they've got 33.3 milliseconds to process the game world, the simulation, all of that stuff," Leadbetter explains. "That's a fair amount of time, but clearly they've decided from a design perspective that they need it. Now, 60fps, you've got to halve that. You've got to do the same job in half the amount of time. It's not viable.".

Sources indicate that PS5 Pro has substantially more GPU power than the base model, allowing it to offer visual enhancements like better resolutions and frame rates across many games. But the massive open world and richly reactive sandbox of a game like GTA 6 is largely handled by the CPU, an area where the PS5 Pro has only a modest advantage over its amateur counterpart.

"The obvious thing is to accept that and say, 'Well, what about 40fps? It's only 10fps more than 30,'" Leadbetter continues. "But that's not the way it works. 40fps in terms of frame time is 25 milliseconds. It's a halfway point between 33 and 16 or 17. That's still a huge amount of optimization or cutbacks specifically that would be required in order to hit a 25 millisecond frame time.".

Why do we care about 40fps at all? Well, most console games target either 30 or 60fps because most modern TVs revision the image 60 times per second. If you get exactly one frame every time the screen refreshes – or one frame every two updates – it's a nice, smooth experience. Anything outside of that range will have a subtle but unpleasant judder.

Sources indicate that however, many of the best gaming TVs refresh 120 times per second – a refresh rate that opens up a smooth 40fps experience as a possibility. 40fps modes offer a notable leap in responsiveness over 30fps games, without as many visual compromises as you'd typically see in a full 60fps performance mode. It's become my preferred way to play in any big, cinematic game that offers the option.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 would be a perfect fit for a 40fps option, but Rockstar's vision is apparently too ambitious to allow for it. "It's just asking for trouble, really," Leadbetter concludes, "in a game that is already so rich and dense, but also a game where literally anything can happen because of the systemic nature of the experience. So 30fps makes sense.".

I want an uglier GTA 6 that runs at 60 FPS – 30 FPS on PS5 and Xbox Series X is more reason to wait for PC.

He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest major action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rockstar Games has today clarified a few remaining details about Grand Theft Auto 6's framerate target and visual settings on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X/S.
  • GTA 6 will be available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming.
  • It has been revealed that you may recall that in early October, a Verge report noted Microsoft had acquired exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6, with the understanding being that the game would be available to stream on any XCloud-supported device - as in, to PC as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rockstar Games has today clarified a few remaining details about Grand Theft Auto 6's framerate target and visual settings on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X/S. And as part of the same announcement, the developer revealed a key detail about the game's cloud streaming options.

GTA 6 will be available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming. However, this is only possible on Xbox Series X/S consoles, as well as - surprisingly - the last generation console, Xbox One. Notably, that means you can't use Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream to PC, or other devices, despite it being useable there.

It has been revealed that you may recall that in early October, a Verge report noted Microsoft had acquired exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6, with the understanding being that the game would be available to stream on any XCloud-supported device - as in, to PC as well. Xbox immediately shot down the report, saying GTA 6 "will not be streaming exclusively or to PC".

Sources indicate that perhaps more surprisingly, the cloud-streamed version will be using Series S graphics settings, not those of the more powerful Series X console. Considering the loss in quality inherent in cloud streaming, this will make for a less-than-ideal way of experiencing the game.

Beyond cloud streaming, GTA 6 supports Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox, so you can stream the game on your local network to any device, from a PS5 or Xbox Series X/S console.

GTA 6 pre-loading is now available across PlayStation and Xbox. The code-in-box physical editions have also started shipping, letting you claim the code and pre-load your copy in time for GTA 6's 19th November launch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marathon is getting a lot bigger next month. In September, Bungie outlined their plans for the shooter making some big promises, namely the arrival of a PvE mode, and now they've shown off what you can expect from its next season, Symbiosis.

Top of the order is that PvE mode, which has a name now: Expedition. It's a roguelite mode, one that's playable in co-op, though a lack of details at this current time doesn't make it clear as to whether you can run it solo or not. The season's trailer, which you can have a gander at below, gives off the impression that you'll have to complete particular tasks before exfiltrating like you normally do. I'm sure we'll learn more in time.

According to recent reports, the previously promised social space will be coming with this revision too, and it's called Limbo. Morbidly appropriate! You can hang out here with your buds, head to a mini arena for some impromptu matches (I think), or head to the firing range where you can test out your weapons. You'll also be able to try out the new runner shell, Bishop, a cooler than you, samurai-sword-wielding robot who can jump real good and do that cool movie thing where it slices a whole bunch of enemies at once in one swing real quick like.

Sources indicate that what will undoubtedly have some folks going "Halo's back!" is the beginning of a beta test for a team deathmatch mode. The Halo comparison is apt not simply because of the fact that it's Bungie who are making it, but because there's a deep-voiced announcer guy talking about all the sick kills you do. Details are slim on how this will work too. Beyond that, there's a few newly introduced weapons to flaunt, and maybe most excitingly, big ole alien enemies to take on.

You've still got a little while to wait for Symbiosis, which is currently slated to launch on December 8th. The game will be free to play from then until December 15th, too, obviously in a bid to show sceptics how good it is now (hopefully it is good, for Bungie's sake).

Sony has issued another system software revision for PS5, and if you want access to any online features, you'll be forced to download and install it.

Yes, this is a required upgrade; it brings the firmware to version 26.07-14.23.00, and is a fairly small 1.3 GB.

In a recent development, what does it do, then? Well, as was the case with the last patch, it has one solitary patch note:.

According to recent reports, the folks at PlayStation have been really cracking down hard on the console's security. This enhancement comes about two weeks after the last, which was also about a fortnight removed from the previous one — an unusually speedy deployment.

Industry observers note that this is for a couple of reasons. The first is that hackers have been jailbreaking the PS5 in fresh and faster ways, utilising generative AI tech to find workarounds and weaknesses in the console's software infrastructure.

Secondly, GTA 6 is on the verge of release.

This is pertinent because, well, it's GTA 6; it's very possible it'll be the biggest game launch of all time. In other words, there's a heightened risk that people will want to hack their PS5 and gain access to the game without paying.

Industry observers note that sony has been making it so that your console must have the latest firmware installed to even boot up GTA 6, and it's highly likely today's revision will indeed be a necessity if you want to play the game. This theoretically minimises the risk of jailbreaking and piracy.

With the game now less than 48 hours away, Sony has sent out one more pre-launch security measure in its battle against hackers.
